source.title: Epistemic Compression: The Case for Deliberate Ignorance in High-Stakes AI

record.tranche_reason: The paper qualifies the scope of double descent, saying its benefits apply to in-distribution performance on a fixed distribution and do not extend to shifted settings. Its own analyses compare model complexity and shifted-data performance, but do not measure a double-descent curve.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses double descent and cites the original work, but does not test the fall-rise-fall pattern, an interpolation threshold, epoch-wise descent, sample-size descent, or a shared effective-complexity predictor. Its simulations and LendingClub/MIMIC-IV analyses report robustness or shifted-distribution outcomes, not the measures named by V1–V7; those results are recorded under fits_no_version. The 15-domain synthesis relies on published results and is not included as a direct test of these versions.
record.test_reason: A perspective piece that mentions double descent (Figure 1b caption, Supp. Note 6) and asserts it applies only to in-distribution performance. It reports no model-size, epoch or sample-size test-error curve and no interpolation-threshold result. Its own analyses (synthetic simulation, LendingClub, MIMIC-IV) measure shifted-distribution robustness across a few model classes. That is a related but different construct, so the study does not test any version. The scope remark is an unsupported assertion, not a result, so T5 does not apply.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that in non-stationary, data-poor (Shifting Regime) domains, extra capacity harms robustness and architectural parsimony should be used. Complexity and scale are viable in stable regimes. Double descent is mentioned only as a stable-regime, in-distribution phenomenon and is not tested. The 15-domain synthesis (13/15 concordance) is called exploratory.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares model classes and shifted-distribution robustness in high-stakes domains; it does not reproduce the original double-descent interventions or measure test error around an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that outcomes differ between Shifting and Stable regimes and describes synthetic robustness as dependent on signal stability (ρ).

fits_no_version.finding: In the synthetic simulation, robust accuracy falls as spurious features are added at rho=0.25 and is flat (benign) at rho=0.8. Results are plotted only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding capacity in the form of spurious features harms shift-robust accuracy when signal stability is low.

fits_no_version.finding: On LendingClub, ΔAUROC from Env A to Env C was +0.039 for FT-Transformer, +0.020 for GBM and −0.020 for 8-feature LR. Robust AUROC was 0.671 for FT-Transformer and 0.674 for LR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-capacity tabular models degrade more under temporal shift than simple expert-feature models.

fits_no_version.finding: On MIMIC-IV, the MLP fell from 0.954 to 0.760 AUROC (worst case 0.740), while LR was 0.733/0.716/0.739 across Env A/B/C. The MLP still had the higher worst-case AUROC.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A high-capacity clinical model degrades more under temporal shift, though its worst-case AUROC can remain higher.

record.problems: The paper does not test any specified double-descent curve or its proposed effective-complexity account. Figure 2 is a simulation with plotted results rather than tabulated values. The authors describe the 15-domain synthesis as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, acknowledge that it lacks a formal risk-of-bias assessment, and note selection and publication limitations.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted from the paper's own reported simulation and LendingClub/MIMIC-IV capacity comparisons recorded here. The 15-domain synthesis and cited studies are not extracted as direct results on the specified double-descent versions.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep of test error and no peak at the interpolation threshold; Figure 1b is a schematic.
No sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold.
No risk curve across model classes past the interpolation point.
D_eff is used for regime scoring, not as a predictor of peak location.
No measurement of noise or regularization effects on a peak.
No re-expression of a double-descent curve by an effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: Record's relation 'tests'/T5 is overturned: the only double-descent content is an asserted scope remark and a schematic figure, so the relation is 'discusses'/T6. Other unsupported asides: Supp. Note 6 says double descent occurs around N≈D_model, without data. The LendingClub capacity ladder had six models, but only three are reported numerically; this is irrelevant to the versions.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size test-error curve or interpolation-threshold peak is measured; the paper reports shifted-distribution robustness comparisons instead.
No test-error trajectory over training epochs is measured.
No training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold is reported.
No cross-model-class risk curve spanning the interpolation point is measured.
Effective dimensionality is discussed and estimated illustratively, but is not tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
The paper discusses noise and regularization, but does not test their effects on double-descent peaks, multiple peaks, or peak disappearance.
The paper defines effective dimensionality but does not re-express a double-descent curve using an effective parameter count.
